title: The woodcutter
hookLine: Huineng, a poor woodcutter who can't read, hears the Diamond Sutra in the market and his mind opens

cards: A young man in a market in the far south of China has just been paid for a load of firewood and turns toward the door.
Near it, a stranger is reciting a Buddhist text out loud, just saying it, the way someone hums at work. The young man stops. He can't read.
And as he listens, the Platform Sutra says, his mind opens. Today, the woodcutter Chan would come to honor as its Sixth Ancestor.

teach.b: First, who he was. His name was Huineng, and the Platform Sutra lets him tell his own story. His father died when he was young.
He and his mother were poor, and he sold firewood in the market to keep them both. He couldn't read or write. Second, what he heard.

teach.h: THE DIAMOND SUTRA IN THE MARKET.
teach.b: The text the stranger was reciting was the Diamond Sutra, a teaching on letting go of fixed ideas, even fixed ideas about the Buddha. Huineng asked where he had learned it.

The man said: on East Mountain, from the teacher Hongren, who tells everyone to keep this sutra. The Platform Sutra says Huineng made sure his mother was provided for, and then walked north to find him.
Third, the first meeting. Hongren asks where he's from and what he wants. Huineng says he's from the far south, and he wants only one thing: to become a Buddha.
Hongren tests him with an insult. You're from the south, a barbarian, he says. How could you become a Buddha?

teach.h: BUDDHA-NATURE HAS NO NORTH OR SOUTH.
teach.b: Huineng answers: people may be from the north or the south, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Fourth, the threshing room. Hongren doesn't praise him.
He sends him to the back of the monastery to split wood and pound rice, and there Huineng works, unnoticed.
Notice where this story puts its turning point: not in a temple hall or a library, but in a market, between a sale and the door, through a stranger who probably never knew.

how: Chan and Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Ancestor, and the Platform Sutra, his story and teaching, is read and taught in Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese temples.

o: a monk who chopped wood as a punishment
Huineng, who heard a sutra while selling firewood
Hongren, the teacher who ran East Mountain

p: sold firewood to keep his mother

s: Huineng read the Diamond Sutra for himself
the Platform Sutra says he couldn't read; he heard it recited.
he first heard the sutra in a temple hall
in a market, after selling his firewood.
Hongren tested him by calling him a southern barbarian
Huineng answered that Buddha-nature has no north or south.

games.q: you're Huineng. the great teacher calls you a barbarian from the south and asks how you could ever become a Buddha. what do you say?
o: people come from north or south, but Buddha-nature has no north or south.
games.why: that's Huineng's answer in the Platform Sutra. Hongren said nothing in praise, and sent him to pound rice.

practice: Choose a sentence you've heard so often you've stopped hearing it: a saying from your family, a line from a prayer, a phrase from a song.
Say it silently and slowly, as if a stranger in a market had just said it, and stay a few breaths with whichever word stands out. If nothing opens, that's fine; you've listened.
